SEC24A-01.note: Plural irregular subject 'larvae' plus habitual present set by 'whenever ... drops' gives 'are'. 'is' is attractive to a reader who takes 'larvae' as singular; the tense cue sits beyond the four-word window.

SEC24A-02.note: Verb agrees with 'pastures' (plural, not 'grass'); the agent pronoun refers back to 'the field vole' (singular). 'is avoided by it' is strong via attraction to 'grass'; 'are avoided by them' pulls on the plural 'pastures'.

SEC24A-03.note: Head noun 'lining' is singular despite the compound 'esophagus and stomach' in its modifier; present tense set by 'if the burning returns'. 'are examined' is the strong attraction distractor.

SEC24A-04.note: 'Harvest after harvest' takes a singular verb, and 'some sixty years ago' requires simple past, excluding the present perfect. 'were meager' attracts readers who hear the phrase as plural.

SEC24A-05.note: Compound subject 'scion and ... rootstock' takes 'have' and the plural pronoun 'their'. 'have its own' is attractive because of the distributive sense ('each has its own') and the 'its' already in the subject.

SEC24A-06.note: Elliptical clause echoes 'have appeared', so the auxiliary is 'has' (singular head 'form'). 'does' is strong because singular do-substitution sounds natural, but it mismatches the present-perfect antecedent.

SEC24A-07.note: 'whether ... had warmed' is an indirect question inside a statement, so it ends with a period; the next independent clause starts a new sentence. The question mark is the strong distractor; comma splice and fused sentence fill the rest.

SEC24A-08.note: A participial phrase giving the result of the main action is set off by a comma. No comma misreads 'root leaving'; the colon before a participle phrase and the period-fragment are the weaker options.

SEC24B-01.note: Ellipsis of 'resist' (from 'resists') needs do-support, and the head 'kinds' is plural: 'do not'. 'does not' attracts via 'sandstone' and the parallel singular 'Basalt resists'; 'is/are not' fail because the antecedent is a lexical verb.

SEC24B-02.note: Singular 'rotor' with a parenthetical three-part list between subject and verb; present tense from 'as two engineers watch'. 'are being tested' is attracted by the list.

SEC24B-03.note: Plural head 'measurements'; present tense from 'unless ... is removed'. 'is overstating' attracts via 'summit' and the following 'its'.

SEC24B-04.note: Plural head 'Samples'; past tense from 'until a supply ship reached'. 'was sealed' attracts via 'core'.

SEC24B-05.note: Singular 'housing' takes 'shields'; the object pronoun refers to 'the sensors', so 'them'. 'shield them' attracts via the plural fronted clause ('sensors', 'girders'); 'shields it' via 'housing'.

SEC24B-06.note: The participle 'migrated', placed after an interrupting clause, needs perfect 'has' (singular 'dune'); intransitive 'migrate' rules out passive 'was'. 'have' attracts via 'lake beds'; 'was' via the past-tense context.

SEC24B-07.note: Two independent clauses ('The lava lake ... cooled'; 'within a decade ferns had rooted') need a semicolon. The colon is the nearest rival but the second clause is a later event, not an explanation; no punctuation invites attaching 'within a decade' to 'cooled'.

SEC24B-08.note: Compound predicate with one subject ('welder ground ... and refilled'), so no comma before 'and'. 'seam, and' is the attractive distractor (comma reflex before a conjunction); 'and,' is never right here.

SEC24C-01.note: 'Everything' is singular, and the past 'found' in the conditional sets a past-habitual main clause: 'was forfeit'. 'were forfeit' is strong (plural 'shelves' and a subjunctive feel); 'is' pulls on the present-tense 'statutes list'.

SEC24C-02.note: Singular head 'practice' (not 'cards'); 'before the railway reached them' sets a past frame, excluding the present perfect. 'were spreading' attracts via 'cards'; 'has been spreading' gets the number right but the tense wrong.

SEC24C-03.note: Plural 'screens'; 'when a new owner emptied' requires simple past, excluding 'have been removed'. The present-tense 'lists' in the concessive clause makes the present perfect attractive.

SEC24C-04.note: Plural 'pigments' takes 'match', and the comparison is to the pigments of the other copies, so plural 'those'. 'matches those' attracts via 'copy'.

SEC24C-05.note: Plural 'tablets' takes 'are'; the possessive refers to the shrine (singular), so 'its'. 'are their' attracts by echoing 'tablets', but no plural antecedent owns the record.

SEC24C-06.note: A direct question with the base verb 'stop' needs do-support; the singular head 'west tower' takes 'does'. 'do the' attracts via 'cathedrals'/'towns'; 'is/are' fail with the bare 'stop', which sits outside the four-word window.

SEC24C-07.note: An introductory infinitive phrase ('To transcribe the interviews') is followed by a comma before the main clause. Without the comma 'interviews the volunteers' reads as a garden path; the period leaves a fragment; 'the,' is garbled. Note: the inserted slang sentence breaks the passage's flow.

SEC24C-08.note: With three translators, the name is restrictive (it identifies which translator), so no punctuation. Paired commas or dashes would wrongly mark it nonessential and are strong distractors; comma plus dash is mismatched.

tells: In every tense grid that pairs a present-perfect option with simple past under a past time clause (SEC24A-04, SEC24C-02, SEC24C-03), simple past is the key and the 'has/have been' options always lose. A test-taker who learns 'perfect never wins when the past is offered' scores all three without reading the time clause, though SEC24A-06 and SEC24B-06 (perfect keys) keep it from spreading to auxiliary items.

Attraction is uniform: in every agreement item the key agrees with the distant head noun and never with the noun nearest the blank (SEC24A-02, SEC24A-03, SEC24B-02, SEC24B-03, SEC24B-04, SEC24C-02, SEC24C-04). A student who applies 'reject the option matching the nearest noun' strikes a distractor every time.

In the verb+pronoun 2x2 grids (SEC24A-02, SEC24A-05, SEC24B-05, SEC24C-05) the key never pairs verb number and pronoun number the same way twice in a predictable pattern, so I found no letter or shape tell there. Key letters across the set look spread (A, B, C, D all appear several times).

Punctuation items have no fixed winning mark: period (SEC24A-07), comma (SEC24A-08, SEC24C-07), semicolon (SEC24B-07), no punctuation (SEC24B-08, SEC24C-08). The no-punctuation option wins twice, so 'the plainest option' is a weak tell only in SEC24B-08 and SEC24C-08.

verb number crossed with pronoun or demonstrative number
elliptical auxiliary echoing an earlier verb
past versus present perfect under a past time clause, with number crossed
plural head noun followed by singular of-phrase, number crossed with tense
singular head with a compound or list inside its modifier
auxiliary choice decided by a verb form far from the blank

phase2_note: All 24 keys match my cold answers (0 cold misses); every explanation's path produces the key and handles each distractor correctly. No per-item drops. Batch-level concerns, not grounds for a single-item drop: (1) in SEC24A-04, SEC24C-02 and SEC24C-03 the present-perfect options always lose to simple past, so a student could learn 'perfect never wins' from the pattern; vary this in future batches. (2) SEC24C-07 has weak distractors and a stray mid-passage sentence ('The speakers often used harbor slang...') that interrupts the split/check sequence. It is grammatical, but the passage should be smoothed before serving.
